items.stem: Which term describes the following: “A stage of sleep with rapid eye movements, fast low-voltage EEG activity similar to waking, and the most vivid dreaming”?
options: NREM sleep
Hypnagogic state
REM sleep
Electroencephalograph (EEG)
items.answer: REM sleep
items.markingKey: REM sleep: a stage of sleep with rapid eye movements, fast low-voltage EEG activity similar to waking, and the most vivid dreaming. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Dement and Kleitman’s study belongs to the biological approach. Reason (R): It measured physiological activity (brain waves and eye movements) to investigate dreaming. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Physiological measurement is the reason it is biological. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): REM sleep is the deepest stage of sleep. Reason (R): In REM sleep the EEG shows fast, low-voltage activity. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: A is false (stages 3–4 NREM are deepest); R is true. [1]

items.stem: Lina is spending a night in a sleep clinic in Dhaka. The EEG shows slow, high-voltage waves for 40 minutes, followed later by fast, low-voltage activity with rapid eye movements. Explain why researchers record eye movements as well as brain waves.
items.answer: Rapid eye movements distinguish REM from other stages with similar EEG (such as stage 1), so REM can be identified accurately.
items.markingKey: 1 mark distinguishes REM; 1 mark accuracy [2]

items.stem: Lina is spending a night in a sleep clinic in Lisbon. The EEG shows slow, high-voltage waves for 40 minutes, followed later by fast, low-voltage activity with rapid eye movements. (a) Identify the stage of sleep shown by the slow, high-voltage waves. (b) Explain why researchers record eye movements as well as brain waves.
items.answer: (a) Deep (stage 3/4) NREM sleep. (b) Rapid eye movements distinguish REM from other stages with similar EEG (such as stage 1), so REM can be identified accurately.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark distinguishes REM; 1 mark accuracy [2]

items.stem: Jonas is spending a night in a sleep clinic in Colombo. The EEG shows slow, high-voltage waves for 40 minutes, followed later by fast, low-voltage activity with rapid eye movements. (a) Identify the stage shown by the fast, low-voltage activity with rapid eye movements, and state what Jonas is likely to report if woken then. (b) Explain one reason why Jonas’s sleep in the clinic may not represent normal sleep.
items.answer: (a) REM sleep; Jonas is likely to report a vivid dream. (b) The unfamiliar setting, electrodes and wires may make it harder to sleep normally (first-night effect), lowering ecological validity.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark REM; 1 mark dream recall [2] (b) 1 mark reason; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “The stages of sleep without rapid eye movements, including deep sleep with slow, high-voltage EEG waves”?
options: Biological approach
Hypnagogic state
Electroencephalograph (EEG)
NREM sleep
items.answer: NREM sleep
items.markingKey: NREM sleep: the stages of sleep without rapid eye movements, including deep sleep with slow, high-voltage EEG waves. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “People only dream in REM sleep.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Dreams are much more likely to be recalled from REM, but some dream reports occur after NREM awakenings (11 of 160 in Dement and Kleitman).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between REM and NREM sleep.
items.answer: REM sleep has rapid eye movements, fast low-voltage EEG activity and vivid dreams; NREM sleep has no rapid eye movements and, in deep stages, slow high-voltage waves with little dream recall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark REM; 1 mark NREM, contrasted [2]

items.stem: Daniel repeated Dement and Kleitman’s procedure with 6 participants in Kuala Lumpur: each was woken ten times from REM sleep and ten times from NREM sleep, and dream recall was recorded. Table: Awakenings with a dream recalled (out of 10) — REM awakenings: 8, 9, 8, 10, 9, 9. NREM awakenings: 1, 2, 0, 1, 1, 2. Name the experimental design used in this study and explain one weakness of using this design here.
items.answer: Repeated measures: the same participants take part in both conditions. Weakness: order effects (practice, fatigue or boredom) may affect performance in the second condition.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct design; 1 mark: weakness explained in context [2]

items.stem: Samuel is spending a night in a sleep clinic in Kuala Lumpur. The EEG shows slow, high-voltage waves for 40 minutes, followed later by fast, low-voltage activity with rapid eye movements. (a) Identify the stage shown by the fast, low-voltage activity with rapid eye movements, and state what Samuel is likely to report if woken then. (b) Explain why researchers record eye movements as well as brain waves.
items.answer: (a) REM sleep; Samuel is likely to report a vivid dream. (b) Rapid eye movements distinguish REM from other stages with similar EEG (such as stage 1), so REM can be identified accurately.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark REM; 1 mark dream recall [2] (b) 1 mark distinguishes REM; 1 mark accuracy [2]

items.stem: “Dement and Kleitman’s (1957) study of sleep and dreams has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including quantitative data in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (the use of EEG): The EEG and eye-movement recordings were objective, quantitative measures, so REM and NREM sleep were identified scientifically rather than by the researchers’ opinion; this increases validity and reliability. Strength (quantitative data): The number of awakenings with dream recall could be compared directly: 152 of 191 REM awakenings versus 11 of 160 NREM awakenings gave clear support for the link between REM and dreaming. Weakness (the validity of dream reports): Dream recall was self-reported: participants may have forgotten or reconstructed details on waking, and judging whether a coherent dream was reported involved some interpretation. Weakness (ecological validity): Participants slept in a laboratory attached to electrodes and were woken by a doorbell several times a night, so their sleep and dreaming may not be the same as at home. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. items.stem: Assertion (A): Dement and Kleitman found a positive relationship between REM duration and the length of dream reports. Reason (R): The number of words in dream narratives tended to be greater after longer REM periods. Choose the correct option.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Participants in Dement and Kleitman’s study were always told whether they were being woken from REM or NREM. Reason (R): Researchers wanted to avoid demand characteristics. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

Participant E (REM): dream recalled 16, no dream recalled 7; Participant A (REM): dream recalled 13, no dream recalled 6. Calculate the percentage of awakenings for Participant E (REM) that were “dream recalled”. Give your answer to one decimal place.

items.stem: Evaluate Dement and Kleitman’s (1957) study of sleep and dreams, including a discussion of ethics.
items.answer: Strength (the use of EEG): The EEG and eye-movement recordings were objective, quantitative measures, so REM and NREM sleep were identified scientifically rather than by the researchers’ opinion; this increases validity and reliability. Strength (ethics): Participants were volunteers who knew they would be woken and recorded; the procedure was not physically harmful and the data were kept confidential. Weakness (ethics): Being woken repeatedly during the night disrupted participants’ sleep, which could cause tiredness and distress the next day, so they needed the right to withdraw. Weakness (generalisability): Only nine adults took part (seven men and two women), and five were studied intensively, so the sample is small and may not represent everyone’s sleep. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

By a doorbell ringing near the bed
By a bright light

items.stem: A student writes: “Dement and Kleitman found that dream recall was equally likely from REM and NREM sleep.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Recall was reported on about 80% of REM awakenings but only about 7% of NREM awakenings.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Describe the three aims (hypotheses) of Dement and Kleitman’s study.
items.answer: To test whether (1) dream recall is greater after REM awakenings than NREM awakenings; (2) the estimated length of a dream relates to the length of the REM period; (3) the pattern of eye movements relates to the content of the dream.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each aim [3]

items.stem: Aisha repeated Dement and Kleitman’s procedure with 8 participants in Hanoi: each was woken ten times from REM sleep and ten times from NREM sleep, and dream recall was recorded. Table: Awakenings with a dream recalled (out of 10) — REM awakenings: 7, 8, 8, 5, 4, 4, 4, 5. NREM awakenings: 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 4, 2, 2. What is the median score for the REM awakenings condition?

Lucas repeated Dement and Kleitman’s procedure with 7 participants in Istanbul: each was woken ten times from REM sleep and ten times from NREM sleep, and dream recall was recorded. Give your answers to one decimal place. (b) Describe one variable that should be controlled in this study and explain why.
items.answer: (a) REM awakenings: 5.9; NREM awakenings: 1.4. (b) The same waking method (a doorbell) for every awakening, so that the way of waking does not affect recall.

items.stem: Evaluate the view that dreaming can be studied scientifically. In your answer, you may refer to self-report, ecological validity and objectivity.
items.answer: Arguments for: Dement and Kleitman used EEG and eye-movement recordings, which are objective and allow REM to be identified reliably. Hypotheses were tested with controlled awakenings and quantitative comparisons (REM versus NREM recall). Arguments against: The content of dreams can only be known through self-report, which may be inaccurate or reconstructed. The laboratory setting may change how people sleep and dream. Eye movements and dream content were matched by interpretation. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Omar repeated Dement and Kleitman’s procedure with 9 participants in Auckland: each was woken ten times from REM sleep and ten times from NREM sleep, and dream recall was recorded. Table: Awakenings with a dream recalled (out of 10) — REM awakenings: 7, 8, 9, 7, 6, 6, 7, 7, 5. NREM awakenings: 2, 1, 2, 4, 0, 2, 3, 3, 1. (a) Identify the independent variable (IV) and the dependent variable (DV) in this study. (b) Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results. (c) Name a suitable type of graph to display the mean scores for the two conditions, and justify your choice. (d) Suggest one improvement to this study and explain how it would improve the validity or reliability of the results. (e) Explain why a independent measures design might have been used instead, and one problem this would cause.
items.answer: (a) IV: whether participants were woken from REM or NREM sleep. DV: the number of awakenings out of 10 on which a coherent dream was reported. (b) The REM awakenings condition had a higher mean (6.9) than the NREM awakenings condition (2.0), suggesting that dreaming is much more likely to be recalled from REM sleep than from NREM sleep. (c) Bar chart, because the IV has separate (discrete) categories, so the mean for each condition is shown as a separate bar with gaps between bars. (d) Use a larger sample with more participants in each condition, so that anomalous individuals have less effect and the results are more reliable and generalisable. (e) Independent measures avoids order effects and makes it harder to guess the aim, but participant variables between the two groups could then explain the results, and more participants are needed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: IV; 1 mark: DV, operationalised [2] (b) 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2] (c) 1 mark: bar chart; 1 mark: justification (discrete conditions / categories, not continuous data) [2] (d) 1 mark: improvement; 1 mark: how to do it; 1 mark: effect on validity/reliability explained [3] (e) 1 mark: advantage of the alternative design; 1 mark: problem it causes; 1 mark: applied to this study [3]

items.stem: Explain why the small sample in Dement and Kleitman’s study is a weakness.
items.answer: With only nine adults (mostly male), individual differences in sleep could strongly affect the results, and the findings may not generalise to women, children or the wider population.

items.stem: Lina reads that Dement and Kleitman’s participants slept in a laboratory with electrodes on their scalp and near their eyes. (a) Explain how this could reduce the validity of the findings. (b) Suggest how a modern researcher could investigate dreaming with higher ecological validity. items.answer: (a) Sleeping in an unfamiliar place with electrodes may change normal sleep patterns and dreaming, so findings may not reflect typical sleep (low ecological validity). Psychological factors such as recent experiences also shape dream content. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: ‘The biological approach provides the best explanation of dreaming.’ Evaluate this statement, using evidence from psychology. In your answer, you may refer to reductionism and REM sleep.
items.answer: Arguments for: Dreaming is strongly associated with a measurable physiological state (REM sleep) that occurs in regular cycles. Eye movements appeared to match the visual content of dreams. Arguments against: Biological measures do not explain the meaning or content of dreams. Some dreams were recalled after NREM awakenings. Psychological factors such as recent experiences also shape dream content. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: accurate, detailed psychological knowledge (named studies/theories) used to build a two-sided argument; evaluation includes issues such as validity, reliability, generalisability, ethics or usefulness; a justified conclusion. Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Explain one practical application of Dement and Kleitman’s findings.
items.answer: Because REM can be identified objectively by EEG and eye movements, sleep clinics can study dreaming and diagnose sleep disorders without relying only on self-report.
items.markingKey: 1 mark application; 1 mark link to findings [2]

items.stem: Outline one strength of Dement and Kleitman’s (1957) study of sleep and dreams that relates to quantitative data.
items.answer: The number of awakenings with dream recall could be compared directly: 152 of 191 REM awakenings versus 11 of 160 NREM awakenings gave clear support for the link between REM and dreaming.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant strength linked to quantitative data; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

A sleep laboratory in Accra replicated part of Dement and Kleitman’s study. 8 volunteers were each woken ten times during REM sleep and ten times during NREM sleep on different nights, and the number of awakenings on which a dream was recalled was recorded. Table: Awakenings with a dream recalled (out of 10) — REM awakenings: 8, 6, 8, 6, 8, 7, 6, 7. NREM awakenings: 1, 10, 1, 0, 1, 2, 2, 1. (a) Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results. (b) Explain one ethical issue that the researcher should consider in this study.
items.answer: (a) The REM awakenings condition had a higher mean (7.0) than the NREM awakenings condition (2.3), suggesting that dreaming is much more likely to be recalled from REM sleep than from NREM sleep. (b) Protection from harm: repeated waking disrupts sleep, so participants should be allowed to withdraw.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2] (b) 1 mark: ethical guideline named; 1 mark: applied to this study [2]

items.stem: “Dement and Kleitman’s (1957) study of sleep and dreams has more strengths than weaknesses.” Evaluate this view, including the use of EEG in your answer.
items.answer: Strength (ethics): Participants were volunteers who knew they would be woken and recorded; the procedure was not physically harmful and the data were kept confidential. Strength (the use of EEG): The EEG and eye-movement recordings were objective, quantitative measures, so REM and NREM sleep were identified scientifically rather than by the researchers’ opinion; this increases validity and reliability. Weakness (ethics): Being woken repeatedly during the night disrupted participants’ sleep, which could cause tiredness and distress the next day, so they needed the right to withdraw. Weakness (ecological validity): Participants slept in a laboratory attached to electrodes and were woken by a doorbell several times a night, so their sleep and dreaming may not be the same as at home. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Which term describes the following: “A recording of eye movements using electrodes placed around the eyes”?

items.answer: Electro-oculogram (EOG)

items.stem: Explain why Dement and Kleitman’s study is an example of the biological approach.
items.answer: It explains a psychological experience (dreaming) in terms of physiological activity, using EEG measures of brain waves and eye movements.

items.stem: Freya is spending a night in a sleep clinic in Singapore. The EEG shows slow, high-voltage waves for 40 minutes, followed later by fast, low-voltage activity with rapid eye movements. Explain one reason why Freya’s sleep in the clinic may not represent normal sleep.
items.answer: The unfamiliar setting, electrodes and wires may make it harder to sleep normally (first-night effect), lowering ecological validity.

items.stem: Describe the findings about eye movements and dream content.
items.answer: Mainly vertical eye movements matched dreams of looking up and down (such as climbers on a cliff, or climbing ladders); horizontal movements matched watching two people throw tomatoes at each other; few movements matched watching something far away, such as driving.

items.stem: Ines wants to find out whether people who are woken from REM sleep report more vivid dreams than people woken from NREM sleep. Plan a laboratory experiment to investigate this. Your plan must include: how the dependent variable will be measured, the sampling technique, the experimental design and controls.
items.answer: Method: a laboratory experiment. Manipulate the IV in a controlled room; standardised procedure and instructions; measure the DV objectively. Variables: IV: REM or NREM awakening; DV: vividness rating 1–10. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Hanoi, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Define the term ‘REM sleep’.
items.answer: A stage of sleep with rapid eye movements, fast low-voltage EEG activity similar to waking, and the most vivid dreaming.
items.markingKey: REM sleep: a stage of sleep with rapid eye movements, fast low-voltage EEG activity similar to waking, and the most vivid dreaming. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]
